explanation: Warmer sand produces mostly females and cooler sand mostly males, so a hot beach can tilt a whole season's hatchlings towards females.

claims.text: In sea turtles, the temperature of the nest during incubation determines the sex of the hatchlings.
In sea turtles, hatchling sex is not decided by the father's genes, the mother's age or the size of the egg.
In sea turtles, warmer incubation temperatures produce more females and cooler ones more males.
Hot nesting beaches can produce hatchlings that are overwhelmingly female.

evidence.restatement: Sea turtles have temperature-dependent sex determination: the nest temperature sets the hatchlings' sex.
Sea turtle sex is not set by the father's genes, the mother's age or the egg's size.
Warmer nests produce more females and cooler nests more males.
Very warm nesting beaches can produce almost all-female hatchlings, as found for northern Great Barrier Reef green turtles.
